excerpt: After reviewing these authorities, we hold that continued employment should not as a matter of law be disregarded as consideration sufficient to uphold a covenant not to compete.
note: Puritan-Bennett Corp. v. Richter, 8 Kan. App. 2d 311 (1983), rev. denied; subsequent Kan. Sup. Ct. opinion 235 Kan. 251 (1984) recites that the Court of Appeals found continued employment sufficient. Qualification: sufficiency is a question of fact (there, seven years of continued employment).

excerpt: In the present case, because Samet was an at-will employee, the plaintiff's forbearance of its right to terminate his employment could be valid consideration if it altered his at-will status.
note: Dur-A-Flex, Inc. v. Dy, 349 Conn. 513 (2024). Court reaffirmed Roessler v. Burwell that a promise of indefinite continued employment can be adequate consideration, and rejected the trial court's categorical 'never' rule, but said bare continuation of at-will status (no promise of any duration) 'seems unlikely' to be adequate (n.45) and remanded. 'Yes' overstates: mere continued at-will employment, by itself, is doubtful under Dur-A-Flex.

excerpt: The oral employment agreement was modified or altered by adding the non-compete agreement. That alteration of the oral contract was done in writing. Under the terms of SDCL 53-8-6 no additional consideration was necessary.
note: Central Monitoring Service, Inc. v. Zakinski, 1996 SD 116, 553 N.W.2d 513. Mechanism: no new consideration needed because a written non-compete alters the existing employment contract (SDCL 53-8-6), not because continued employment is itself consideration. Court noted a 'completely new', stand-alone contract would need new consideration.

excerpt: Non-compete agreements entered into by existing employees may be supported by independent consideration. For example, an employer may provide an employee with a raise or promotion in exchange for signing a non-compete agreement.
note: Access Organics, Inc. v. Hernandez, 2008 MT 4, 341 Mont. 73. Court rejected employer's argument that continued employment and salary sufficed (distinguishing Langager) and held the afterthought agreement lacked good consideration.

excerpt: We hold that an employer that forbears from terminating an existing at-will employee forbears from exercising a legal right, and that therefore such forbearance constitutes adequate consideration for a noncompetition agreement.
note: Lucht's Concrete Pumping, Inc. v. Horner, 255 P.3d 1058 (Colo. 2011). Opinion text read from a vLex reproduction (Justia/CourtListener blocked), hence secondary tier. Caveat not verified against primary: 2022 amendments to C.R.S. 8-2-113 (notice to current employees keyed to consideration) have prompted commentary that Lucht's may be narrowed; no appellate ruling found.

excerpt: If the agreement is entered into after commencement of employment but not in connection with the separation from employment, it must be supported by fair and reasonable consideration independent from the continuation of employment
note: M.G.L. c.149, s.24L(b)(ii); applies to agreements entered on or after Oct. 1, 2018.

excerpt: The existence of sufficient consideration to support a post-employment restraint may be found in either the original contract of employment or in a post-employment contract, where the supporting consideration is at least, in part, the continuation of employment.
note: Hogan v. Bergen Brunswig Corp., 153 N.J. Super. 37 (App. Div. 1977), reversing 151 N.J. Super. 344 (Ch. Div.), which had held continued employment insufficient. Intermediate appellate authority; covenant there was a non-solicitation, and the court relied partly on ~3 years of continued employment.

excerpt: Therefore, we adopt the rule that when a covenant is entered into after the inception of employment, separate consideration, in addition to continued at-will employment, is necessary in order for the covenant to be enforceable.
note: Poole v. Incentives Unlimited, Inc., 345 S.C. 378 (2001).

That § 3–716(a)(1)(i)2 and (b) ... shall be construed to apply only to employment contracts ... executed on or after July 1, 2025. ... this Act shall take effect June 1, 2024.
